Price lists, stock checks, shipping quotes per city, matching bank-transfer screenshots… all by hand. For a small florist, that means missed orders and lost custom requests.

One loan. Fourteen sites. Five countries.
In September 2024, two lenders agreed a US$30 million green loan for BECIS Bioenergy. An accordion could add US$20 million. The total would reach US$50 million.

The loan supports 14 bioenergy installations. They are in Indonesia, Thailand, Cambodia, the Philippines and India. They turn agricultural waste into steam. The steam is sold to commercial and industrial customers under long-term offtake agreements.

Small units look risky one by one. Repeated across a portfolio on one contract type, they can become one credit story.

The public sources give no tenor, no pricing and no per-site capacity. So we draw no conclusion on terms.

What the deal shows is the logic. A repeatable offtake contract can matter more than the size of one site.

For a developer with several small projects, the question is simple. Could your sites be financed together, on one contract template?

COP31 Türkiye, Day 4 – Antalya  

Disinformation is a story, not just a wrong fact. I started the day at the PRAXIS project launch on societal resilience in an age of climate disinformation. In a hands-on exercise, we compared how wildfires in Türkiye, the UK, and Brazil get blamed on developers, politicians, or NGOs. I shared Australia's version. The panellists Rabia Karakaya Polat, Seda Demiralp, Thiago S. Gouvêa Lago Dominguez Teles, and Silvia Maria Manfredi made the key point: disinformation functions as a narrative with villains, victims, and someone to blame. Their evidence shows that how easily people fall for disinformation has little to do with politics and a lot to do with how well they cope with uncertainty. 

AtEvidence for Climate Action (E4CA), Sven Harten moderated a sharp panel, and the message was to start from the decision you want to inform, not from the research question. I asked how academics can get involved, and it was great to receive helpful information from all the panellists and a chat with Sven afterwards.

Blue carbon is far more complicated than I had thought. The ASEAN Pavilion session on financing ASEAN's blue economy showed how many threads have to come together for a mangrove project. You need comprehensive, measurable ecological data and clear land rights for coastal communities that own the land. The project also has to earn international recognition for its carbon credits and deliver real financial return for investors, with Indonesia's new regulation aiming to make communities shareholders rather than just landowners who are paid rent. 

At Innovating Finance and disability inclusive climate action at the Australia Pavilion,Sainimili Tawake of the Pacific Disability Forum said people with disabilities are not passive recipients but architects of adaptation. The speakers also called for "15% for 15%: putting 15% of budgets toward inclusion, matching the share of people living with disability. The practical example of early warnings for disability is also impressive.

In 2022 my job was getting releases out. In 2025 part of my job was showing a bank's change management process that a release was ready to go out.

Between those two dates I was a release engineer at Vascomm from June 2022, ran a small software house from July 2023, and from January 2025 worked on-site as a DevOps engineer at Bank Syariah Indonesia, building CI/CD on OpenShift.

At the bank, a release did not move on a green pipeline alone. The automated security checks had to pass before production, and the approval step needed deployment evidence that someone could read without an engineer beside them.

Since then I ask three questions of any release:

1. What exactly was deployed?
2. Which checks ran against it, and did they pass?
3. Who approved it, and when?

That is why I am now looking at technology risk and IT audit roles. The pipeline was the part I built. The evidence was the part other people relied on.

For people in change management or IT audit: when you review a release approval, which piece of evidence do you open first?

Precast Concrete Pile Construction: Beyond Installation Productivity

Drawing on my experience in foundation engineering at PT Frankipile Indonesia in 2017 and PT Keller Franki Indonesia, I have learned that successful piling construction involves much more than driving concrete piles into the ground.

Precast concrete piles are designed to transfer structural loads through weaker soil layers into deeper strata with sufficient bearing resistance. However, their performance depends on several interconnected engineering and construction factors.

From a senior civil engineer's perspective, I believe there are six critical aspects to consider:

1. Geotechnical Investigation and Design

Understanding soil conditions is the starting point of foundation engineering. Borehole investigations, SPT results, groundwater conditions, and soil parameters are essential for determining pile capacity, length, settlement, and installation requirements.

2. Manufacturing Quality Control

Pile quality starts at the production stage. Concrete strength, reinforcement arrangement, prestressing, curing, and dimensional tolerances must comply with the approved specifications. Proper quality control is essential to ensure that piles can withstand handling, transportation, and installation stresses.

3. Transportation and Installation

Lifting, handling, and storage require careful attention. During installation, pile alignment, hammer selection, driving energy, penetration records, and splicing quality must be closely monitored to prevent structural damage.

4. Pile Driving and Geotechnical Behaviour

One important engineering principle is that driving resistance is not necessarily equal to the pile's actual static bearing capacity. Final set, blow count, soil resistance, and hammer performance must be evaluated together with the design assumptions and appropriate verification methods.

5. Testing and Quality Verification

Static Load Tests, Pile Driving Analyzer (PDA), and Pile Integrity Tests (PIT) provide different types of information about foundation performance. Understanding their purposes and limitations is essential when evaluating whether installed piles meet the design requirements.

6. Construction Management and Productivity

Daily installation quantities should never be the only measure of contractor performance. Equipment efficiency, material quality, pile damage, rework, safety, cost, and technical compliance must also be considered.

My key lessons learned:

A properly designed pile can still underperform because of poor installation. Likewise, high installation productivity does not necessarily indicate successful foundation construction.

Ultimately, successful piling construction is not measured by how many piles are installed, but by how reliably they perform as part of the permanent structure.

By the Numbers: 14 open federal construction notices are for work outside the United States, in nine countries, and all 14 are Department of War.

Not one open VA notice and not one open GSA Public Buildings Service notice names a place of performance outside the United States.

Where the 14 are:
Peru 3
Germany 2
Italy 2
Japan 2
Australia, Djibouti, Norway, the Philippines and the United Kingdom, one each

All three Peru notices belong to the USACE Latin America and Caribbean District.

Only three of the 14 take a priced offer today:
N4008426R7500, NAVFAC Far East, design-build RMAC facility improvement at NETDC, Zambales, Philippines, due Dec 1
FA568226R0007, Air Force 31 CONS, Construction Basic Ordering Agreement, Aviano Air Base, Italy, due Jun 8, 2027
FA558724R0003, Air Force 48 CONS, Tri-Base Area Construction Basic Ordering Agreement, RAF Lakenheath, United Kingdom, due Apr 27, 2029

The other 11 are sources sought, presolicitations or special notices.

The clock trap: six of the 14 carry a response clock set to a zone other than the project country's own. A Royal Australian Air Force base apron and taxiway project closes on Honolulu time. A Chabelley Airfield power plant project in Djibouti closes on Eastern time. The Zambales design-build closes on Jakarta time, an hour behind Manila.

14 is a floor, not a total. In the same open field, 211 notices leave the place-of-performance country blank, and a blank is not a statement that the work is domestic. One example is a live buy: W912ER26RA016, Apache Alert Mission Complex, a construction solicitation from the USACE Middle East District with no set-aside stated, proposals due 8 January 2027, and an empty place-of-performance record.

What to check: search by contracting office, not by country. Convert the deadline from the offset the notice carries, not from the project's city. And read the whole notice for the place of performance, because on an overseas buy the country field is often empty and the location sits in the body or the attachments.

Our read: overseas past performance is bought from a short list of buying offices, and five of the nine countries hold exactly one open notice each. Getting on that list is a relationship with an office, not a response to a market.

Source: the SAM.gov daily Contract Opportunities extract, downloaded November 18, 2026, and the PIEE daily construction and A-E file of the same date. The calendar said 17:30. That's 23:30 where I sit.

I run Kogentic from Jakarta, with a small remote team and developers we're learning from across Europe and the US. A developer just booked a user interview on our European calendar. The slot looked civilised: 17:30. Then I did the conversion. 11:30 for the person joining from the US. 23:30 for me. Nobody did anything wrong. The time was right for them. It just wasn't evening for all three of us.

I said yes anyway. I'll be on the call, and I asked an AI notetaker to join as backup. Not to run it. Just so the notes don't depend on how sharp I am at 23:30. We're building software for developers who work like this — across time zones, with AI in the loop — and it would be a bit rich to preach that and then dodge the late one.

The lesson I keep relearning: a calendar time is always someone's local time, and rarely everyone's. The work is deciding whose clock you're willing to honour, and how you still show up when it's yours that loses. What's the latest call you've taken because the other person's 17:30 wasn't yours?

A message queue stores messages until they're consumed, but the Jakarta Messaging standard deliberately leaves some behavior undefined, including how long a queue keeps messages and what happens when resources overflow. Worth knowing before you rely on it.

#MessageQueue #Messaging #DistributedSystems #Constraints #SystemDesign #SoftwareEngineering #BackendDevelopment #Reliability #Architecture #Developers #TechCommunity #LessonsLearned

More info
• Expiration has limits. An undelivered message that reaches its expiration time should be destroyed, and clients shouldn't receive expired messages. But the standard doesn't guarantee they won't, and it defines no notification when a message expires.

• Priority is best effort too. There are ten levels, 0 to 9, with 0 to 4 as normal and 5 to 9 as expedited. A provider doesn't have to enforce strict priority ordering; it only has to do its best to deliver expedited messages ahead of normal ones. #JakartaMessaging #Priority
